questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Cartesian Function With Respect to Plane Polar Coordinates
questions.problem: Given that $w(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2},$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂w}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=x,\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =-(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +0\,(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $h(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & ={r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =3{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $g(x,y)={y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂g}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta } & =0\,(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )+(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $w(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}),$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =(\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{2r({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{2}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=r(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1),$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂y}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $g(r,\theta )={r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{∂g}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r}=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,\,\frac{∂g}{∂\theta }=-3{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(-3{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =r(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta -3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $w(r,\theta )=r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{∂w}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(r,\theta )=r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂f}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r}=\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=2r+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂x}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=2,\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =(2)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2r}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2yz,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y+2z\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2z)r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $u(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+xyz,$ find $\frac{∂u}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $u(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =\frac{∂u}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂u}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂u}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂u}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $u$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂z}=2{x}^{2}z+xy\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2{r}^{2}z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}(2z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $v(x,y,z)=2y-xz,$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $v(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂v}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂v}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂v}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂v}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂v}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂v}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂x}=-z,\,\frac{∂v}{∂y}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂x} & =-z, \\ \frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta } & =-(-z)r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2)r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =rz\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=xy+{y}^{2}z+x{z}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+2xz\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Cartesian Function With Respect to Plane Polar Coordinates
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\dfrac12x^2+y^2,$ find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta,$ where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Polar Function With Respect to Cartesian Coordinates
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $w(r, \theta)=r \cos 3\theta,$ find $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}\cos\theta - \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta}\sin\theta
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta +3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Cartesian Function With Respect to Cylindrical Polar Coordinates
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $w(x,y,z)=z^3(x^2+2y^2),$ find $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\cos\theta, y=r\sin\theta,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂w}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=2x{z}^{3},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=4y{z}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =2r{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =4r{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =-(2r{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(4r{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-2{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
